results.title: Crop-specific approaches for innovative and collaborative on-farm trialing approaches systematically use simpler, yet larger-scale evaluations, and capture gender-disaggregated data, for a more farmer- and market-relevant selection of new crop varieties
results.description: In recent years, there has been a concerted effort by regional Breeding networks to validate the performance of new candidate crop varieties under farmer conditions to ensure they meet the needs of farmers. However, this process is challenging due to the logistics involved in mass producing seed/clones, distribution and the need to sample a representative set of farmers in the target environment across multiple countries with different implementing partners with different capacities. In recent years, new approaches to scalable on farm verification such as Triadic Comparison of Technologies (TRICOT) have been developed and piloted for both seed and clonal crops. Other methods employing non-replicated, sparse testing models have also been piloted across a range of crops and pipelines. This result assesses the organizational change across crops. In 2025, 95% of breeding programs conducted on-farm verification in at least one pipeline utilizing a methodology that met minimum standards. In 2026, best practices will be harvested from across these efforts to develop a standard, scalable and cost effective strategy for all regional breeding networks.

results.title: Rooted Apical Cuttings - cost-effective method for potato seed production in Sub Saharan Africa
results.description:
Work on rooted apical cuttings (RAC) has been featured in the poverty section of the CGIAR Flagship Report 2025, responding to the decision-maker question: “How can we stimulate rural job opportunities within agrifood systems for young people and women?”

RACs provide a low-cost, high-multiplication alternative for early-generation seed production, addressing several critical challenges, including high seed costs and low multiplication rates, weak early-generation seed systems, and limited rural employment opportunities.

Public-sector stakeholders—such as national ministries and local governments—are increasingly interested in embedding RACs into seed systems. For example, Ministries of Finance view RACs as a pathway to economic growth, job creation, and poverty reduction driven by local agricultural production, while Ministries of Agriculture emphasize their role in improving seed quality, boosting agricultural productivity, and reducing dependence on imported seed. These outcomes are central to national food security and rural development goals.

Similarly, the private sector sees RACs as a high-return investment opportunity within scalable and sustainable agricultural models that offer long-term growth and profitability. Seed producers and agri-tech companies can increase production efficiency by adopting cost-effective, locally sourced RACs, expand market reach, and integrate innovative technologies to further enhance productivity.

results.title: Market-driven validation protocols for rice varieties tested across South Asia and Africa by IRRI and partners
results.description: Rice breeding programs often struggle to develop varieties that meet diverse market demands and farmer preferences across different regions. To address this challenge, the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) and partners developed systematic validation protocols that test new rice products against popular local varieties in real farming conditions. These protocols were applied across seven priority market segments in India, Bangladesh, Nepal, Kenya, Tanzania, and Mozambique, validating 21 new rice products through on-farm trials and farmer participation methods. The approach compares new varieties directly with existing market-dominant options, generating reliable evidence about performance and farmer preferences. In Kenya, this validation process contributed to the official release of three IRRI rice varieties by the Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization. The protocols provide agricultural agencies and policymakers with evidence-based methods to accelerate adoption of improved rice varieties that better match market needs and farming conditions.

results.title: SEED BRIDGE partnership model developed by IRRI to accelerate rice variety adoption through improved seed systems in Asia and Africa
results.description: Rice farmers often lack access to improved varieties due to weak seed supply chains and limited partnerships between breeding programs, seed producers, and markets. IRRI developed the SEED BRIDGE partnership model to address this challenge by creating multi-stakeholder platforms that connect breeding organizations, national partners, private seed companies, seed millers, traders, and regulators. The model was tested through 18 strategic partnerships in India, Bangladesh, and Nepal, resulting in the production and distribution of 7,400 kg of high-quality breeder and foundation seeds. These partnerships strengthened early-generation seed production systems and supported small-scale seed enterprises, including farmer-producer companies and cooperatives, to become self-reliant. The SEED BRIDGE model facilitates germplasm access, creates market linkages, and accelerates the commercialization of newly validated rice varieties, ultimately improving farmers' access to better seeds and promoting faster varietal turnover.

results.title: Protocol for the Inspection and Certification of Quality Declared Seed (QDS) to be used by QDS producers themselves to self-declare the quality of their seed
results.description: Quality seed certification is often a bottleneck for smallholder seed producers, particularly for vegetatively propagated crops like cassava. The International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA) developed this digital protocol to enable seed producers to self-assess and declare the quality of their cassava planting material. The methodology combines digital tools including Seed Tracker and PlantVillage Nuru applications, allowing producers to conduct quality assessments and transmit results electronically to Tanzania's Official Seed Certification Institute in real-time. This innovation addresses the challenge of expensive and time-consuming traditional certification processes. The protocol is being tested with 20 quality declared seed producers in Tanzania, with careful attention to gender balance in participant selection and analysis.

results.title: Genome-edited rice varieties with enhanced nitrogen use efficiency developed by IRRI for improved yields in the Philippines
results.description: Rice production faces challenges from inefficient nitrogen use, leading to reduced yields and environmental concerns. The International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) developed genome-edited rice varieties that better accumulate and utilize nitrogen within the plant. Using targeted gene editing techniques, researchers modified genes involved in nitrogen metabolism to enhance the plant's ability to redistribute nitrogen from leaves to grains during development. This innovation was applied to both transplanted and direct-seeded rice varieties commonly grown by farmers. The enhanced nitrogen use efficiency aims to increase rice yields while maintaining grain quality, potentially reducing fertilizer requirements and supporting more sustainable rice production systems.

The enhanced network enables more effective development and testing of rice varieties suited to direct seeding methods across different climatic and soil conditions.

results.title: Economic viability of scaling improved bean technologies in Burundi and Zimbabwe
results.description: Scaling improved bean varieties and complementary technologies are important to improve crop productivity incomes and food and nutrition security in Sub‐Saharan Africa. In Burundi and Zimbabwe, bean technologies were promoted through a demand‐led and public–private partnership model. While econometric approaches have been used to estimate the impact of enhanced technologies on farmers' livelihoods for a long time, no economic feasibility analysis has been done. Most analyses focus on farmers livelihoods, overlooking other value chain actors like traders, processors, and seed producers including community seed multipliers. Thus, this study contributes to the literature by conducting an economic feasibility analysis that includes all actors in the bean value chain and estimates additional investments attracted from public and private stakeholders. We further identified gains or losses on account of the externalities generated through different value chain actors. We find positive net present values (NPV) and a benefit–cost ratio (BCR) greater than one. This implies that the economic benefits of the bean value chain improvement program in the two countries are larger than their costs. Farmers and traders are the main beneficiaries, receiving 99% and 65% of the net economic benefits generated in the bean value chain in Burundi and Zimbabwe, respectively. Finally, we find the intervention sustainable and resilient against economic shocks, making it worth replicating in other countries in sub‐Sahara Africa and beyond. Pragmatic and policy options are recommended to inform future interventions of a similar nature.

results.title: Development of DNA markers for assisted selection of cassava resistant to cassava mosaic disease (CMD)
results.description:
Cassava is an important staple crop in tropical and subtropical regions. Cassava mosaic disease (CMD) is one
of the most dangerous diseases affecting cassava production in Africa. Since the first reported in Southeast Asia in 2015, the CMD prevalence has become a concern in Southeast Asia. To combat it, CMD resistance has been introduced from African cassava into Asian elite cultivars. However, efficient DNA markers for the selection of CMD resistance are not available. The CMD2 locus confers resistance to African cassava mosaic virus via non-synonymous substitutions in the DNA polymerase δ subunit 1 gene (MePOLD1). Here, we developed DNA markers to identify the mutations providing the resistance. We examined the association between the resistance score in CMD-infected fields and the genotypes of hybrids of CMD-resistant and ‑susceptible Asian lines. Our study provides powerful tools to the global cassava breeding community for selecting CMD resistant cassava.

results.title: Training on heat-tolerant and iron-rich common bean breeding advances shared with Central American researchers
results.description: The Alliance of Bioversity and CIAT presented research progress on developing common bean varieties that can withstand high temperatures while maintaining high iron content to researchers participating in the Central American Cooperative Program for Crop and Animal Improvement. The presentation shared findings from field evaluations showing how certain bean materials maintain stable yields under heat stress through improved nutrient production and seed filling efficiency. The research also demonstrated successful breeding strategies that combine high-yielding varieties with iron-rich genetic sources, producing stable lines with enhanced nutritional value. This knowledge sharing enables Central American breeding programs to develop climate-resilient bean varieties with improved nutritional quality, addressing both climate change adaptation and malnutrition challenges in the region where beans are a staple food crop.

results.title: Determination of rice accession status using infochemical and visual cues emitted to sustainably control diopsis apicalis dalman
results.description: This study assessed the host plant selection behavior of female stalk-eyed flies (SEFs) or Diopsis apicalis, where a Y-tube olfactometer was used to compare SEF attraction to the odor of leaves from four rice varieties (ITA306, WAB56-104, CG14, and RAM55). Another step of the evaluation consisted of pairing leaf odors from two rice varieties. Also, potted plants of the tested varieties were displayed in a screened cage and submitted to female SEF selection. The results indicated that the odor produced by leaves from rice varieties CG14, WAB56-104, and ITA306 significantly attracted SEFs, at rates of 81%, 70%, and 97%, respectively, while SEF females were rarely attracted by the odor of leaves from the resistant rice variety RAM55, at a rate of 35%. The results suggested that the use of a Y-tube olfactometer was similar to the use of a screened cage. The resistance exhibited by rice variety CG14 against SEFs is related to an antibiosis interaction acting as bait, while that in RAM55 is an antixenosis one. Farmers can plant the traditional CG14 variety on the edge of rice fields to draw SEFs and poison their larvae. However, RAM55 can be inserted in an intercropping system to repel SEFs from laying eggs. The authors recommend CG14 and RAM55 as candidates for breeding to create resistant lines against SEF.

results.title: Genetic structure of Ethiopian finger millet landraces and genome-wide association mapping for agronomic and nutritional traits
results.description: Finger millet (Eleusine coracana subsp. coracana) (2n = 4x = 36) remains one of the most important millets in East Africa (EA), where it was most likely domesticated along the highlands of Ethiopia and Uganda. The goal of the current study was to understand the population structure of the Ethiopian finger millet landraces and identify quantitative trait nucleotides (QTNs) and haplotypes associated with agronomic and nutritional traits. In a field evaluation across three environments, 448 genotypes were assessed for days to flowering (DTF), days to maturity (DTM), thousand seed weight (TSW), grain yield (GY), stay-green score (STG), and drought score (DrtSc). The harvested grain was analyzed for Fe and Zn contents. A subset of 391 genotypes was skim-sequenced, generating 24,112 high-quality SNPs that were employed for population structure, association mapping, and haplotype analysis. Seventy marker-trait associations were detected including 15 major QTNs with more than 30% phenotypic variance explained (PVE) for all traits except STG and GY. Pleiotropic major QTNs were identified for DTM/DTF and Fe/Zn on chromosomes 9B and 2B, respectively. Haplotype analysis of major QTNs identified 54 significant haplotype blocks and 2 additional haplotypes for a multidrug ABC transporter gene family like protein on chromosome 4A that was associated with PTH. Favorable haplotypes from pleiotropic DTM/DTF and Fe/Zn QTNs were present in 13 and 12 genotypes respectively, majority from Tigray region. Two genotypes from Tigray and one from Amhara harbored favorable haplotypes for DTM/DTF and Fe/Zn. These findings provide invaluable insights for targeted breeding to enhance finger millet resilience, nutritional profile, and yield.

results.title: Molecular screening of septoria-resistant genes in historical Turkish bread wheat germplasm using the validated gene specific SSR markers
results.description: Septoria tritici blotch (STB), caused by Zymoseptoria tritici, poses a significant threat to global wheat production, particularly in Türkiye. Resistance breeding is the most sustainable and effective disease control method. Molecular markers, especially simple sequence repeat (SSR) markers are extensively employed in wheat breeding to enhance the efficacy. The primary objective of this study was to identify Stb resistance genes among 143 historical registered Turkish bread wheat genotypes released as commercial cultivars between 1963 to 2014, using 16 closely linked SSR markers. The findings revealed substantial genetic variation among the screened cultivars, with the Stb3 gene being the most prevalent, identified in 89.51% of the samples. Other notable resistant genes included Stb13 (71.32%), Stb4 (43.33%), and Stb11 (41.25%). Cultivars Porsuk-2811, Porsuk-2853, and Porsuk-2868 exhibited the highest level of resistance to STB, with 10 resistance genes detected. Of the 143 cultivars screened, 10 were found to carry a total of nine Stb genes, while two cultivars were observed to possess only a single resistance gene. The study identified 23 wheat cultivars harboring 8-10 Stb resistance genes, which are highly recommended for future wheat breeding programs and gene pyramiding strategies to combat Z. tritici. This research provides critical insights for national breeding programs, supporting the development of resilient and high-yielding wheat varieties resistant to STB.

results.title: Market intelligence guided rice seed market segmentation and product design in Tanzania
results.description: Rice seed companies in Tanzania transformed their market approaches by implementing segmentation strategies based on comprehensive market intelligence provided by CGIAR's International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) through the Breeding for Tomorrow initiative. The market intelligence identified distinct farmer segments with varying needs, purchasing power, and preferences, enabling companies to design targeted seed products and marketing strategies. This evidence-based approach replaced previous one-size-fits-all marketing methods, helping companies better serve smallholder farmers, commercial producers, and different regional markets across Tanzania. The segmentation framework considers factors such as farm size, income levels, rice varieties preferred, and seasonal planting patterns, ultimately improving seed accessibility and adoption rates among diverse farming communities.

results.title: Resilient yet productive: maize that can thrive under stress and in optimal conditions
results.description: In the Asian tropics, maize is predominantly grown as a rainfed crop during the summer-rainy season, which often suffers significant yield losses due to the erratic distribution pattern of monsoon rain that causes intermittent dry spells and/or excessive moisture within the season. The climate-induced abiotic stresses, particularly drought and waterlogging, pose significant threats to rainfed maize cultivation in the Asian tropics, where erratic patterns of monsoon rain and associated high genotype-by-environment interaction (GEI) effects undermine yield stability. To address these challenges, this study evaluated 61 advanced-stage maize hybrids developed under the Asia Waterlogging and Drought Tolerant (AWDT) product profile, designed to deliver hybrids with stable grain yields under variable moisture regimes without yield penalties under optimal conditions. Multi-environment trials (METs) were conducted across 19 locations in South and Southeast Asia (India, Bangladesh, Vietnam, and Thailand) under four moisture regimes: optimal, rainfed/random stress, reproductive-stage drought, and vegetative-stage waterlogging. A stratified ranking approach was employed to identify superior hybrids that matched or exceeded commercial checks under optimal conditions and outperformed them under at least one stress environment. Several elite hybrids demonstrated broad or specific adaptation to targeted stress-prone environments. These findings underscore the importance of targeted breeding and MET-based selection strategies in developing high-performing stress-resilient maize cultivars for climate-vulnerable agroecologies, with implications for food security, farmer livelihoods, and sustainable cropping systems in the face of escalating climate variability.

results.title: Decision support for managing an invasive pathogen through efficient clean seed systems: Cassava mosaic disease in Southeast Asia
results.description:
Context
Effective seed systems must distribute high-performing varieties efficiently, and slow or stop the spread of pathogens and pests. Epidemics increasingly threaten crops around the world, endangering the livelihoods of smallholder farmers. Responding to these challenges to food and economic security requires stakeholders to act quickly and decisively during the early stages of pathogen invasions, typically with limited resources. A current threat is the introduction of cassava mosaic virus in Southeast Asia.

Objectives
Our goal in this study is to provide a decision-support framework for efficient management of healthy seed systems, applied to cassava mosaic disease. The specific objectives are to (1) evaluate disease risk in disease-free parts of Cambodia, Lao PDR, Thailand, and Vietnam; (2) incorporate estimated risk of disease establishment with seed exchange survey data and whitefly spread in the landscape to model epidemic spread; and (3) identify candidate regions to be prioritized in seed system management.

Methods
We used machine learning to integrate disease occurrence, climate, topology, and land use, and network meta-population models of epidemic spread. We used scenario analyses to identify candidate priority regions for management.

Results and conclusions
The analyses allow stakeholders to evaluate strategic options for allocating their resources in the field, guiding the implementation of seed system programs and responses. Consistently targeting initially high priority locations with clean seed produced more favorable outcomes in this model, as did prioritization of a higher number of districts for the deployment of smaller volumes of clean seed.

Significance
The decision-support framework presented here can be applied widely to seed systems challenged by the dual goals of distributing seed efficiently and reducing disease risk. Data-driven approaches support evidence-based identification of optimized surveillance and mitigation areas in an iterative fashion, providing guidance early in an epidemic, and revising recommendations as data accrue over time.

results.title: Exploring the multifaceted dynamics of flowering time regulation in field crops: Insight and intervention approaches
results.description: The flowering time (FTi) plays a critical role in the reproductive success and yield of various crop species by directly impacting both the quality and quantity of grain yield. Achieving optimal FTi is crucial for maximizing reproductive success and ensuring overall agricultural productivity. While genetic factors undoubtedly influence FTi, photoperiodism and vernalization are recognized as key contributors to the complex physiological processes governing flowering in plants. Identifying candidate genes and pathways associated with FTi is essential for developing genomic interventions and plant breeding to enhance adaptability to diverse environmental conditions. This review highlights the intricate nature of the regulatory mechanisms of flowering and emphasizes the vital importance of precisely regulating FTi to ensure plant adaptability and reproductive success. Special attention is given to essential genes, pathways, and genomic interventions geared toward promoting early flowering, particularly under challenging environmental conditions such as drought, heat, and cold stress as well as other abiotic stresses that occur during the critical flowering stage of major field crops. Moreover, this review explores the significant progress achieved in omics technologies, offering valuable insights and tools for deciphering and regulating FTi. In summary, this review aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the mechanisms governing FTi, with a particular focus on their crucial role in bolstering yields under adverse environmental conditions to safeguard food security.

results.title: Yield and climatic parameters in a common bean (Phaseolus vulgaris L.) regional trial
results.description: Abstract Understanding patterns of crop response to environmental factors is critical to simulating target environments in selection environments. In early stages of varietal development, breeding lines are usually developed in centralized facilities. Subsequently, testing continues on a broader array of research stations before dissemination to farmers, fields. Such a system is practiced in common bean ( Phaseolus vulgaris L.) breeding in East Africa. A regional yield trial called the East Central Africa bean yield trial was distributed in three separate groups that aligned with three breeding pipelines: Andean bush beans (Group 1 or G1), Mesoamerican bush beans (G2), and climbing beans (G3). Forty‐three trials met minimal standards of data quality. Trial environments composed of a site, planting date, and its climatic parameters were clustered based on 13 variables of temperature, rainfall, relative humidity, vapor pressure deficit, and altitude. Climatic data were derived from the NASA Prediction of Worldwide Energy Resources (POWER) database, which estimates day‐by‐day weather for each site. Four climate clusters emerged from this analysis. Climbing bean yield corresponded to climate clusters and heavily responded to high altitude and temperature. Most Andean bush bean environments occupied a centric cluster with few extreme variables. No patterns were observed in the Mesoamerican bush beans. This method should be extended to a larger set of trials and should be used to compare research station environments with farmer production environments.

results.title: Pathogen-Informed Strategies for Durable Resistance in Rice: Lessons from Bacterial Blight
results.description: Bacterial blight (BB), caused by Xanthomonas oryzae pathovar oryzae (Xoo), is a major rice disease in Asia and Africa. Xoo possesses virulence factors for pathogenicity and race differentiation that complicate resistance breeding of rice. The availability of 48 BB resistance (R) genes (Xa/xa) portends the selection of R genes for broad and durable resistance. To establish durable resistance, understanding the pathogen virulence spectrum and host resistance mechanisms is required. This review examines the global distribution and diversity of Xoo populations, highlights the different resistance mechanisms of 15 Xa/xa genes, and identifies the three effective resistance genes for 24 countries. The review proposes strategies for durable, broad-spectrum resistance to BB.

results.title: Genomic analysis reveals the interplay between ABA-GA in determining fresh seed dormancy in groundnut
results.description: Groundnut is an important oilseed crop; however, its productivity and seed quality are frequently reduced due to lack of fresh seed dormancy (FSD). To address this challenge, a mini-core collection of 184 accessions was phenotyped to identify potential donors in each agronomic type. In addition, whole genome re-sequencing and multi-season phenotypic evaluations were analyzed to identify stable marker-trait associations (MTAs) linked to FSD. Phenotypic analysis revealed substantial variability in dormancy durations, with days to 50 % germination (DFG) ranging from 1 to 30 days. Multi-locus genome-wide association study (ML-GWAS) identified 27 MTAs in individual seasons and 12 MTAs in pooled seasons data, respectively. Key candidate genes identified included Cytochrome P450 superfamily proteins, protein kinase superfamily proteins, and MYB transcription factors involved in the Abscisic acid (ABA) pathway, as well as F-box interaction domain proteins, ATP-binding ABC transporters, associated with the Gibberellic acid (GA) pathway. SNP-based KASP (Kompetitive Allele-Specific Polymerase chain reaction) markers were developed for 12 SNPs, of which four markers (snpAH00577, snpAH00580, snpAH00586 and snpAH00588) were found useful for the selection of FSD. The combination of favourable allele from four genes namely Ahfsd1 (Arahy.8B3CAL), Ahfsd2 (Arahy.NRZN5K), Ahfsd3 (Arahy.JJ8FJQ), and Ahfsd4 (Arahy.PI0JM6) provides stable 24–30 days of dormancy. Incorporating favourable dormant alleles into breeding programs could enable the development of high-yielding cultivars with a dormancy period of more than two weeks.

results.title: Fortifying crops with micronutrients for sustainable global nutritional security
results.description: The adverse effects of climate change on crop productivity and nutritional content have raised concerns toward food and nutritional security. These challenges can be mitigated by developing climate-resilient and biofortified crop varieties. A biofortification strategy focused on developing cultivars enriched in essential micronutrients is one of the most promising and effective approaches to addressing nutrient deficiencies in the context of a changing climate. Current efforts by scientists around the globe are aimed at bio-fortifying crops to meet present and future nutritional security needs. The grain fortification with enhanced mineral content in the seed endosperm/cotyledon depends on several factors: the nutritional status of the soil, the bioavailability of minerals in the rhizosphere, and, more specifically, the plant's ability to efficiently uptake and transport these nutrients to the sink organs. Microorganisms play a critical role in this process by improving soil health and facilitating the breakdown of trace elements through various biogeochemical cycles. In particular, plant growth-promoting (PGP) microbes, primarily actinomycetes, enhance bioavailability of minerals to crop plants, thereby improving seed mineral content. Emerging technologies and research innovations can combat global hidden hunger, and ensure nutritional security worldwide, even amidst the challenges posed by climate change. This review highlights the importance of biofortification, addresses the imminent challenges, and suggests actionable solutions. Additionally, it explores the combination of traditional agricultural practices with modern approaches to enhance nutritional quality of crops, thus contributing to a sustainable and secure food system for the future.

results.title: Training regulatory authorities in Tanzania on improved diagnostics for seed testing
results.description: The Tanzania Official Seed Certication Institute (TOSCI) is the national regulatory authority responsible for managing the quality of seed. As part of this role, they apply diagnostic methods to test for the major diseases that affect seed quality. For cassava, the two main biotic constraints to seed quality are the virus diseases - cassava mosaic disease and cassava brown streak disease. TOSCI currently has quantitative Polymerase Chain Reaction (qPCR) capacity at its headquarters in Morogoro, central Tanzania, which can be used to test for these viruses in pre-basic disease. However, TOSCI has an aim to decentralize this testing as well as to reduce the cost so that it can better serve its seed producer clients. IITA supported TOSCI towards achieving this goal by running two training events in 2025. The first was for run in southern Tanzania (Mtwara) from May 12-16 while the second was run in Mwanza in north-western Tanzania from September 8-15. Both trainings were successfully implemented and TOSCI now has improved loop-mediated isothermal assay (LAMP) diagnostic capacity in both north-western and south-eastern Tanzania, to complement existing capacity at its HQ. LAMP has the advantage of being both cheaper and partially-portable, when compared to the standard qPCR.

results.title: Women seed-grower's training on quality hybrid maize seed production in Nepal
results.description: Two rounds of women-focused hybrid maize seed growers trainings were successfully conducted in Dang district, Nepal, during December 2024 and November 2025, contributing to strengthened local capacity for quality hybrid seed production and enhanced women’s leadership in the seed sector. Across both training events, a total of 140 participants were trained, of whom 80% were women, reflecting a deliberate effort to promote gender inclusion in high-value agricultural enterprises. The trainings were designed to build practical and entrepreneurial skills among smallholder farmers and emerging seed producers, with a strong emphasis on empowering women to engage competitively in hybrid maize seed value chains. Participants received hands-on instruction covering the complete hybrid seed production cycle, including field selection, parental line management, planting ratios, detasseling techniques, rouging, pest and disease management, harvesting, post-harvest handling, seed drying, storage, and basic marketing principles. Field-based demonstrations and peer learning were integral components of the training approach. The initiative aligned with CIMMYT’s broader efforts to promote women-led hybrid maize seed production in Nepal, as highlighted in recent CIMMYT documentation on women’s growing role in strengthening domestic seed systems. Collaboration with local institutions, extension services, and private seed companies helped link trainees to technical backstopping, input support, and market opportunities, including buy-back arrangements that reduced production and marketing risks. The trainings have contributed to increased confidence and technical competence among women seed growers, enabling many participants to engage in contract seed production or initiate their own seed enterprises. By strengthening local hybrid seed production capacity and expanding women’s participation in seed markets, the initiative supports Nepal’s goals of reducing dependence on imported hybrid seeds, improving farm incomes, and building a more inclusive and resilient maize seed system.

results.title: Advancing variety positioning and placement through farmer-centered approaches
results.description:
To achieve objectives set under the B4T's Inclusive Delivery Position for Demand, cross-country evidence for varietal placement and commercialization was generated through farmer-led activities. The Dryland Crops Program, together with partner NARS, INERA (Burkina Faso), ABU and LCRI (NIgeria), ISRA (Senegal) and IER (Mali) jointly nominated and evaluated superior released varieties and advanced breeding lines of sorghum, pearl millet, and groundnut in the four countries. Tricot trials and demonstration plots were establisehed across the four countries using seven to thirteen varieties per crop, depending on country context, under farm conditions. A total of 690 farmers participated directly in trial implementation and evaluation. These trials generated comparative, farmer-validated performance data across multiple agro-ecologies, strengthening the evidence base for variety placement and product advancement decisions.
This evidence-driven approach supported early market signals, leading to the identification and formal request of three sorghum varieties and one pearl millet variety by stakeholders in Nigeria. Over time, this result is expected to contribute to faster, lower-risk commercialization and more efficient cross-country scaling of priority varieties.

results.title: Strengthening soybean seed value chains in Mozambique
results.description:
Soybean is a crop with growing importance in Mozambique and is providing increasing numbers of farmers with opportunities to increase their incomes and improve their livelihoods. To drive this growth opportunity, farmers need access to good quality seed of high yielding varieties. IITA worked with the national research system (IIAM), private sector partners and communities to strengthen the soybean seed system. To replace old low-yielding varieties, the breeding team has produced a range of improved materials, and five new variety releases were completed in December 2025
(G18) TGx 1835-10E (10E)
(G13) TGx 2001-24FM (Bela)
(G01) TGx 2002-35FM (Ovilela)
(G15) TGx 2014-21FM (Ulimi)
(G12) TGx 2014-16FM (Malonda)
Seed deployment of improved varieties was enhanced through the production of 28 tons of foundation seed, and 680 tons of farmer-preferred seed produced by community based seed producers. A partnership with the regulatory authorities ensured that quality standards were upheld. Further progress is anticipated in 2026 as 45ha of the new varieties will be planted. Following harvest they will be introduced into the seed system for further multiplication, with the expectation that this will result in yet higher yields and sustained improvements to the livelihoods of all those associated with soybean value chains in Mozambique.

results.title: Improving policy, regulation, and practice in Rwanda's seed sector: Validation of an analysis of Rwanda's seed regulatory system
results.description: Under Rwanda’s Strategic Plan for Agriculture Transformation (PSTA4) and its successor plan (PSTA5), efforts are being made to accelerate seed sector growth and encourage greater private investment. CGIAR Centers--working with MINAGRI, NSAR, NML, and partners—continue to support reforms to Rwanda’s seed regulatory system and enabling environment for private sector investment. Emphasis is placed on addressing issues that are particularly important to private seed companies and entrepreneurs: (i) early generation seed production and distribution, (ii) varietal registration and release processes, (iii) seed quality assurance systems, and (iv) seed trade. CGIAR research identifies and communicates potential intervention points, regulatory changes, good practices, and legal innovations that can address farmers’ needs, reduce costs, and accelerate seed sector growth. Activities in 2025 included participation in the high-profile National Seed Congress, publication of new regulatory analyses, and continued engagement with public and private sector stakeholders. Incremental changes in policy and investment priorities indicate that progress is being made towards a more inclusive, innovative, and private sector-driven seed sector in Rwanda.

results.title: Seed Production Hubs for building a sustainable hybrid maize seed market system in Nepal
results.description: Nepal’s maize sector has historically relied heavily on imported hybrid seeds, constraining farmer profitability and weakening national seed system resilience. To address this challenge, CIMMYT, in collaboration with the Nepal Agricultural Research Council (NARC), private seed companies, and local governments, has supported the development of a sustainable hybrid seed market system through targeted local capacity development and market-oriented interventions. A central strategy has been the establishment of hybrid seed production hubs in key maize-growing districts, including Dang, Kapilvastu, and Kailali. These hubs promote coordinated seed production by clustering farmers, improving access to technical support, strengthening quality assurance, and reducing transaction costs for seed companies. Farmers received hands-on training on hybrid seed production protocols, quality control, and post-harvest handling, while private seed companies supplied parental lines, technical supervision, and buy-back guarantees. As part of this effort, six micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) operating in the seed sector were directly supported to enhance their technical, managerial, and market capacities. Support to these MSMEs included improved access to breeder and foundation seed, technical training on hybrid seed production and quality standards, and facilitation of linkages with producer groups, NARC and local governments. Strengthening MSMEs has been critical to anchoring local seed production and expanding commercial distribution networks. The results have been substantial. Domestic hybrid maize seed production increased significantly, production areas expanded, and farmer participation rose markedly. In Dang district alone, locally produced hybrid seed now covers thousands of hectares, and increasing farmer incomes. The intervention has also strengthened women’s participation, particularly in skilled seed production roles. By reinforcing linkages among farmers, MSMEs, research institutions, and the public sector, the initiative has laid a  foundation for an inclusive, resilient, and commercially viable hybrid seed system in Nepal.

results.title: Enhancing the capacity of agrovets to strengthen inclusive and last-mile seed market systems in Nepal
results.description: To strengthen Nepal’s seed market system and improve smallholder farmers’ access to quality seed, CIMMYT organized a series of capacity-building trainings for agrovet owners across five provinces between late 2024 and 2025 under the CGIAR Breeding 4 Tomorrow Initiative. Agrovets — private agricultural input suppliers who sell seeds, fertilizers, pesticides, and tools — play a critical role as the last-mile link between seed producers and farmers, yet many lacked updated knowledge on new varieties, seed quality standards, and national seed regulations. More than 300 agrovet owners from Sudurpashchim, Karnali, Lumbini, and Bagmati provinces participated in the trainings, which were held in collaboration with provincial Agriculture Knowledge Centers and seed testing laboratories. Key topics included awareness of newly released open-pollinated and hybrid varieties, seed quality assurance and safe handling, certification and regulatory procedures, ethical business practices, and strategies for building inclusive, resilient seed systems. A survey conducted during the training highlighted challenges such as limited supply of high-quality local seed, inconsistent awareness of seed regulations, and weak linkages with seed companies. Strengthening agrovet capacity and connectivity with seed value chain actors is essential to ensure farmers receive reliable information and quality inputs. By empowering agrovets with updated technical and business skills, the initiative is contributing to a more inclusive, efficient, and farmer-centered seed market system across Nepal.

results.title: Demand-led seed systems linking traders, producers and farmers increase improved bean variety adoption across seven African countries
results.description: Seven African countries—Cameroon, Ethiopia, Kenya, Rwanda, Uganda, Zambia, and Zimbabwe—have successfully implemented trader-centered seed system models that connect seed producers directly with farmers through market-driven mechanisms. Developed under CGIAR's Breeding for Tomorrow initiative with Alliance of Bioversity and CIAT support, these innovative approaches have increased adoption of improved bean varieties by placing traders at the center of seed distribution networks. Each country adapted the model to local contexts: Zambia and Rwanda established Multi-Stakeholder Platforms with trader leadership, while Uganda and Ethiopia integrated digital tools and export contracts to strengthen market linkages. Key innovations include trader-financed seed production, digital tracking systems, and participatory variety selection that responds to actual market demand rather than supply-driven approaches, demonstrating how market mechanisms can transform traditional seed systems across diverse African agricultural contexts.

results.description: National Agricultural Research Systems in Cameroon, Ethiopia, Kenya, Rwanda, Uganda, Zambia, and Zimbabwe have transformed their traditional supply-driven seed delivery methods to become more responsive to market demands. These institutions now prioritize farmer and trader needs through innovative strategies including trader-centered platforms that bring multiple stakeholders together, digital systems that provide market intelligence, contract-based financing mechanisms, and policy reforms that encourage private sector participation. results.title: Demand-Led, Grain Trader-Centered Seed System: A paradigm shift for Grain Trader-Centered Seed System
results.description: The traditional model of developing and disseminating agricultural seed often follows a linear \"push\" system, where varieties are bred and then offered to farmers with the hope that market demand will follow. The \"Demand-Led, Grain Trader-Centered Seed System\" represents a paradigm shift. This model positions grain traders—the actors with the most direct link to consumer markets—as the central drivers of seed demand. By leveraging their market intelligence and commercial interests, the system aims to create a \"pull\" effect, ensuring that the varieties produced and disseminated are those explicitly demanded by the end-market. This report synthesizes lessons from Rwanda, Zambia, Ethiopia, and Uganda to analyze the significant opportunities presented by this model, as well as the persistent barriers that must be overcome for it to operate at scale.

results.title: Extension services transformed into market facilitators connecting smallholder farmers with inclusive seed systems across eight African countries
results.description: Extension services in Kenya, Uganda, Zambia, Zimbabwe, Burundi, Rwanda, Cameroon, and Ethiopia have evolved beyond traditional agronomic advice to become critical market facilitators in seed delivery systems. Through the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT's Inclusive Delivery Project, extension agents now connect smallholder farmers with traders, seed producers, and processors while ensuring women, youth, and marginalized groups access improved crop varieties. This transformation from supply-driven to demand-led approaches has strengthened multi-stakeholder platforms, reduced adoption risks for farmers, and enhanced seed system resilience. Extension agents use demonstrations, training, and digital tools to align markets with farmer needs, creating sustainable pathways for varietal turnover and improved livelihoods across diverse farming communities.

results.title: A manual for strengthening the technical and operational capacity of seed producers in pearl millet and sorghum hybrid seed  production
results.description: During the reporting period, a comprehensive technical manual on hybrid sorghum seed production was developed to support structured training of seed producers and field technicians. The manual provides end-to-end technical guidance across the hybrid seed production cycle, including parental line management, production planning, field establishment, flowering synchronization, pollination management, quality assurance, harvesting, processing, certification, and traceability. It was designed to address critical technical bottlenecks in hybrid seed production in the region, including limited producer knowledge of hybrid-specific production practices, contamination risks, poor seed set due to synchronization challenges, and weak quality management systems. This is expected to contribute to improved hybrid seed yield, genetic purity, certification compliance, and profitability of hybrid seed enterprises, while supporting increased availability of high-quality hybrid sorghum seed and improved farmer access to high-performing varieties in dryland production systems

results.title: Market-led bean seed systems increased quality seed production across eight African countries
results.description: The Seed Equal initiative implemented market-led bean seed systems in Burundi, Cameroon, Ethiopia, Kenya, Rwanda, Uganda, Zambia, and Zimbabwe from 2022 to 2025. This demand-driven approach significantly increased production of high-quality bean seeds across all categories. Total production reached 468 metric tons of breeder seed, over 4,335 metric tons of foundation seed, and more than 72,819 metric tons of certified seed. Ethiopia became the leading breeder seed producer with over 358 metric tons, while Uganda and Zambia emerged as major certified seed production hubs with nearly 15,000 and over 19,700 metric tons respectively. The Alliance of Bioversity and CIAT contributed to developing these strengthened seed value chains, which improved farmers' access to quality planting materials despite climate challenges like the 2024 drought that temporarily affected some countries.

results.title: Gender inclusion framework developed for bean seed value chains across eight African countries by Alliance of Bioversity and CIAT
results.description: The Alliance of Bioversity and CIAT developed a comprehensive framework examining gender inclusion in market-led bean seed systems across Uganda, Kenya, Rwanda, Burundi, Cameroon, Zambia, Zimbabwe, and Ethiopia. The framework identifies significant gender disparities in leadership roles, resource access, and benefit distribution within seed value chains. While all countries demonstrate intentional gender tracking, women face limited access to capital, underrepresentation in trade leadership, and digital exclusion risks. The framework reveals varying progress levels: Zambia shows strong female participation in seed production, Rwanda demonstrates integrated gender approaches in training, while other countries show basic tracking with limited transformative strategies. This work provides critical guidance for strengthening gender-transformative approaches in seed value chain development across Africa.

results.title: Dvara E-Registry plans to expand IFPRI-co-created digital financial services to 50,000 smallholder farmers across India
results.description: Building on successful impact evaluations in Odisha, Dvara E-Registry is preparing to scale innovative digital financial services co-developed with IFPRI to reach 50,000 smallholder farmers nationwide. The platform uses satellite imagery and field data to assess creditworthiness based on crops grown rather than land ownership, enabling farmers without land titles to access formal credit and insurance. Initial results demonstrated increased uptake of financial services, higher agricultural profits, reduced farmer stress, and particularly strong benefits for women. The evidence-based approach has strengthened investor confidence, positioning the partnership to embed research-driven innovation into scalable financial systems that enhance smallholder resilience across India's diverse agricultural landscapes.
